opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things I find most fascinating about Picbreeder, because it's really where the human element does something an algorithm couldn't easily do on its own.

When people breed images in Picbreeder, they aren't just picking what looks best right now. Often they pick something because they sense it *could become* something. You see a shape that's a little bit eye-like, or there's some symmetry emerging, and you think, "There's something here. If I keep going, something interesting might come out of this." That's an intuition about potential, not about present quality. And it turns out to be really important, because the stepping stones to interesting things almost never look like the final thing.

The famous example is the car. Someone got a car image, but the ancestor of that car was an alien face. Nobody breeding that alien face was trying to get a car. They chose it because it was interesting, because it seemed to have some kind of richness or promise. Then later someone noticed the eyes looked a bit like wheels, and they followed that. If you had set out with the objective "evolve a car," you would never have selected the alien face, because it doesn't look like a car at all. So the objective would have actually blocked you from finding the car.

What the humans bring is a sense of interestingness, a nose for where there might be more to discover. And I think that's deeply connected to the representations underneath. When people choose images with potential, they're often implicitly choosing genomes that have a good underlying structure: symmetry, regularity, modular parts that can be varied in meaningful ways. We saw this when we looked at the internal representations of the Picbreeder networks. They were remarkably well organized, almost factored, so that one part of the network controlled, say, the mouth opening, and another controlled something else. Compare that to networks trained with SGD to produce the same image: the output looks identical but the internals are a tangled mess. That's the fractured, entangled representation idea.

So my interpretation is that human intuition about potential is acting as a kind of filter that favors good representations, even though people have no idea they're doing that. They're responding to what feels open-ended, what feels like it has room to grow, and that correlates with structure that is actually evolvable. That's a lesson for AI more broadly. It's not just about getting the right output; it's about how you got there. The path, guided by this sense of what's interesting and what might lead somewhere, shapes the quality of the representation. And objective-driven optimization, which ignores the path, can end up with something that looks right but is underneath not the kind of thing you can build on.

r001.rationale: The response says users sense an image’s potential while breeding it, but does not state that experience with Picbreeder develops that intuition.

r002.rationale: It explicitly contrasts choosing an image for what it could become with choosing what looks best right now.

r003.rationale: The alien-face-to-car example shows users selecting an image for its promise without aiming at or predicting the specific final image.

r004.rationale: It links human selection to organized, evolvable representations, but does not attribute those representations to successive lock-ins of increasingly complex conventions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the most interesting things about Picbreeder, and I think it's central to what we learned from it. When people are evolving images in Picbreeder, they're not doing it with a target in mind, at least not usually. They're just looking at a set of images and picking the one that they find interesting, or the one that looks like it might lead somewhere. And that word "might" is really doing a lot of work there.

What's happening is that people have this intuitive sense of potential. They look at an image and there's something about it that suggests it could become something, even though it isn't anything yet. Maybe there's a hint of symmetry, or a shape that reminds them vaguely of an eye or a face, and they're not thinking "I'm going to make a face." They're thinking "huh, that's kind of interesting, let's see where it goes." That's the stepping stone intuition. They're recognizing a stepping stone without knowing what it's a stepping stone to.

And I think this is exactly the thing that objective-based search can't do. If you set an objective, you're evaluating everything by how close it is to the target. But the stepping stones to interesting things often don't look like the target at all. The famous example is the car that came out of an alien face. Nobody who was trying to evolve a car would have selected an alien face as a step along the way, but somebody who was just following their intuition about what was interesting did, and then the eyes became wheels. So the human intuition about potential is doing something that a fitness function fundamentally can't, because it's not measuring distance to a goal. It's recognizing richness, or latent structure, or just novelty.

The other thing I'd say is that these intuitions are distributed. No single person in Picbreeder has to have good intuitions about everything. Different people are attracted to different things, and because it's a branching system where you can pick up where someone else left off, you get this kind of collective exploration where everyone's idiosyncratic sense of potential contributes. One person's dead end is another person's starting point. So the diversity of human intuition actually becomes a feature of the search, not noise.

And I think the deep lesson, which is really what Joel Lehman and I ended up writing about in the Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned book, is that this kind of intuition about potential is a legitimate form of knowledge. It's not just whimsy. People are often right that something is interesting, even when they can't articulate why or where it leads. And if we want systems that are genuinely open-ended and creative, we probably need to find ways to capture or approximate that kind of judgment, rather than replacing it with objectives.

r001.rationale: The response describes users using an intuitive sense of potential, but does not say that experience with Picbreeder develops that intuition.

r002.rationale: It contrasts an image’s current state with what it might become, but does not clearly distinguish evolutionary potential from present aesthetic appeal.

r003.rationale: It says users can notice hints such as symmetry or an eye-like shape and follow them without knowing what they will lead to or targeting a specific final image.

r004.rationale: The response does not explain that Picbreeder’s rich representation arises through successive lock-ins of increasingly complex conventions.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting thing is that people can recognize potential without knowing what it’s potential for. In Picbreeder, you’re looking at images and choosing which ones get to have offspring. And you might choose something because it looks intriguing, or because there’s some structure in it that you haven’t seen before. You don’t necessarily have a destination in mind.

You might see something that looks a little like a face and follow that for a while, but then it starts to look like a car, and you go in that direction instead. So your intuition is helping you identify stepping stones, but it isn’t necessarily predicting the final result. It’s more like saying, “There’s something here worth exploring.”

And that distinction matters because we tend to equate potential with progress toward a particular objective. But something can have tremendous potential while looking nothing like the thing it will eventually lead to. If you insist on judging every image by how close it is to the picture you wanted at the beginning, you can actually discard the stepping stones that would have led to something remarkable. What people bring to Picbreeder is this ability to appreciate something interesting before they can explain where it’s going.

r001.rationale: The response describes intuition for spotting worthwhile stepping stones, but does not say that experience with Picbreeder develops that intuition.

r002.rationale: It separates potential from progress toward a preset goal, but does not distinguish potential from an image’s present aesthetic appeal.

r003.rationale: The response says users can notice structure worth exploring without knowing or predicting the eventual result, and illustrates this with an image shifting from a face-like form to a car.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss the underlying representation or the accumulation of increasingly complex conventions through successive lock-ins.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s fascinating is that people aren’t necessarily choosing an image because it’s already something wonderful. They’re often choosing it because they feel there’s something there—some potential that they can’t quite articulate. Maybe it looks a little like a face, or there’s an interesting symmetry, and they want to see where it goes.

That’s different from having a particular image in mind and asking, “Which of these is closest to it?” You’re letting your intuition tell you what’s interesting, and that changes the direction of the search. Something that seems like a detour can become the stepping stone to something you never would have imagined at the outset.

And in Picbreeder, other people can pick up those stepping stones. They might see potential in an image that its original creator didn’t see. So you get this collaborative exploration where nobody has to know the eventual destination. Their local judgments about what’s worth exploring can produce something surprising much later.

r001.rationale: The response describes users relying on intuition about an image’s potential, but does not say that experience with Picbreeder develops that intuition.

r002.rationale: It contrasts choosing an image for its potential with choosing one because it is already wonderful, distinguishing future possibility from present appeal.

r003.rationale: It gives structural cues such as a face-like quality or symmetry and explains that users explore without knowing the eventual destination.

r004.rationale: The response does not attribute Picbreeder’s rich representation to successive lock-ins of increasingly complex conventions.
